analysis.one_liner: Lets the EPA regulate cigarettes under federal toxic-chemical law.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 22 cosponsors from both parties, the bill was sent to a House subcommittee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1976, federal toxic-substances law has deliberately excluded tobacco products. This bill would strike that exclusion, making cigarettes subject to the Toxic Substances Control Act so the EPA could regulate them as chemical substances that pose an unreasonable risk to health. The bill's findings point to the 1986 Surgeon General's conclusion that cigarette smoke causes lung cancer deaths among nonsmokers. The bill never advanced past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Nonsmokers and the public, whose exposure to secondhand smoke the bill aimed to address by giving the EPA authority over tobacco products as toxic substances.

how_it_helps.text: Would make tobacco and tobacco products subject to the Toxic Substances Control Act, letting the EPA regulate them as chemical substances that present an unreasonable risk to health or the environment.
Its findings cite the Surgeon General's 1986 conclusion that a large number of lung cancer deaths among nonsmokers are caused by cigarette smoke.

Would repeal the clause Congress wrote into the 1976 law that excluded tobacco products, closing a gap its sponsors said left the government without the authority needed to deal with the public-health threat of cigarette smoke.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, which would face EPA testing, controls, and enforcement for their core product, with costs that could be passed on to smokers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The Toxic Substances Control Act was written for industrial chemicals; extending it to cigarettes would have handed the EPA broad, untested authority over a legal consumer product, and the bill does not explain how that authority would work in practice.
Compliance with EPA testing and controls would have imposed new costs on tobacco manufacturers, which in a regulated consumer market are typically passed to buyers through higher prices.
Federal restrictions on smoking already existed for airlines under separate laws, so critics could argue a new regulatory pathway was not clearly the most effective tool against tobacco harm.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a documented harm: secondhand smoke killing nonsmokers. But its chosen tool, a chemicals statute, was an untested fit for tobacco, and the practical costs and enforcement questions were never examined because the bill never got past committee. Its promise was real; its design was unproven.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 1990, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then passed to a subcommittee a few weeks later, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Luken introduced the bill on June 28, 1990, with eight original cosponsors including Henry Waxman, Dick Durbin, and Ron Wyden.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On July 16, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials.
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and growers, who stayed outside the EPA's toxic-substances authority, and members of Congress who never had to vote on regulating cigarettes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco makers, which avoided EPA regulation

for.name: Rep. Thomas A. Luken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors including senior committee members.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 16, 1990, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: The industry, the target of the bill, had long opposed expanding federal regulation of tobacco products.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 16 of 257 House Democrats and 6 of 175 House Republicans joined the sponsor — but no vote was ever held, so the parties' positions were never tested on the floor.

industries.note: Cigarettes would become subject to EPA regulation as toxic substances, exposing the industry's core product to testing, controls, and enforcement for the first time under this law. The industry's interest in staying exempt ran against the public's interest in reduced secondhand-smoke exposure.
EPA controls on cigarette products could reduce demand for domestic tobacco leaf and add compliance burdens upstream. The bill never advanced far enough for these effects to be measured.
